varieties.name: Washington Navel
varieties.notes: The classic seedless winter eating orange; easy to peel. Juice turns bitter on standing, so eat it fresh rather than juicing.

varieties.name: Cara Cara
varieties.notes: Pink-fleshed navel: sweeter and lower in acid than Washington, with berry notes. Same winter season and easy peel.

varieties.name: Lane Late
varieties.notes: Late navel that ripens after Washington and holds well on the tree, stretching the navel season into late spring.

varieties.name: Hamlin
varieties.notes: Early, fall-ripening juice orange from Florida; among the more cold-tolerant sweet oranges, often picked before freezes.

varieties.name: Valencia
varieties.notes: The top juice orange; ripens spring into summer and holds on the tree for months. Juice keeps its sweetness.

varieties.name: Moro
varieties.notes: Deepest-colored blood orange, raspberry-tinged. Flesh colors best where winter nights are cool; may stay pale in hot or humid areas.

varieties.name: Trovita
varieties.notes: Thin-skinned, few-seeded orange that sets and sweetens well in hot, dry inland and desert climates where navels struggle.

varieties.name: Seville
varieties.notes: Bitter orange for marmalade and cooking, not fresh eating. Tough, fragrant tree; also a traditional citrus rootstock.

varieties.name: Improved Meyer
varieties.notes: Sweeter, thin-skinned lemon-orange hybrid; the hardiest, most compact lemon and the best choice for pots brought indoors in winter.

varieties.name: Eureka
varieties.notes: The common grocery lemon; nearly thornless and fruits much of the year. Less cold-tolerant than Lisbon; best in mild coastal climates.

varieties.name: Lisbon
varieties.notes: Vigorous, thorny tree with fruit shaded inside the canopy; tolerates heat, wind and cold better than Eureka. Crop more concentrated.

varieties.name: Variegated Pink Eureka
varieties.notes: Eureka sport with cream-striped leaves, striped young fruit and pink flesh; grown as much for looks as for juice.

varieties.name: Ponderosa
varieties.notes: Novelty lemon-citron hybrid with grapefruit-sized, thick-rinded, seedy fruit. Cold-tender; a popular container plant.

varieties.name: Owari Satsuma
varieties.notes: The most cold-hardy mandarin (mature trees take the low 20s °F); seedless, easy-peel, ripens in fall before hard freezes.

varieties.name: Clementine
varieties.notes: Sweet, easy-peel winter mandarin; nearly seedless when grown alone, seedier near other citrus. Tends to bear in alternate years.

varieties.name: Kishu
varieties.notes: Tiny, seedless, very easy-peel mandarins on a small tree; a good container citrus and a favorite with kids.

varieties.name: Gold Nugget
varieties.notes: Seedless, rich, sweet late mandarin with bumpy rind; holds on the tree from late winter into summer.

varieties.name: Pixie
varieties.notes: Seedless, mild, very sweet late mandarin; easy peel and stores well on the tree. Tends to bear in alternate years.

varieties.name: Tango
varieties.notes: Seedless form of W. Murcott: sweet, juicy, easy-peel fruit in late winter to spring, even with other citrus nearby.

varieties.name: Bearss
varieties.notes: The common seedless lime (Persian/Tahiti); larger fruit, milder acid, and about as cold-hardy as a lemon.

varieties.name: Mexican
varieties.notes: True Key lime: small, seedy, intensely aromatic fruit. The most frost-tender common citrus; protect below about 30 °F.

varieties.name: Kaffir
varieties.notes: Grown for its fragrant double-lobed leaves (and bumpy zest) for Southeast Asian cooking, not juice. Tender; good in containers.

varieties.name: Rangpur
varieties.notes: Not a true lime: very sour orange-fleshed fruit used like lime. Notably more cold- and heat-tolerant than true limes.

varieties.name: Finger Lime
varieties.notes: Slender fruit filled with caviar-like juice beads; a garnish crop. Thorny, slow, tolerates part shade; good in containers.

varieties.name: Mexicola
varieties.notes: Small, thin-black-skinned, rich fruit; among the hardiest avocados (mature trees to about 18–20 °F). Type A.

varieties.name: Bacon
varieties.notes: Smooth green, mild fruit in late fall–winter; cold-tolerant to about 24 °F. Type B; a good pollinizer for Hass.

varieties.name: Zutano
varieties.notes: Hardy (to about 26 °F), upright, prolific; light, mild fall–winter fruit. Type B pollinizer for Hass.

varieties.name: Fuerte
varieties.notes: Classic green-skinned winter avocado with rich flavor; hardier than Hass (to about 26 °F). Type B; tends to alternate bear.

varieties.name: Hass
varieties.notes: The standard pebbly black avocado; rich and long-holding. Damaged near 30 °F, so best in frost-free spots. Type A.

varieties.name: Lamb Hass
varieties.notes: Hass-type with larger fruit on a compact, upright tree; ripens after Hass, extending the season into fall. Type A.

varieties.name: Reed
varieties.notes: Large, round, green, buttery fruit in summer–fall that doesn't brown when cut. Upright tree; frost-tender. Type A.

varieties.name: Wurtz
varieties.notes: Also sold as Little Cado: a semi-dwarf (to ~10–15 ft) Hass-like tree, the usual choice for large pots and small yards. Type A.

varieties.name: Chicago Hardy
varieties.notes: Hardiest common fig: regrows from roots after freezes and still fruits on new wood the same year. The pick for zones 5–6.

varieties.name: Celeste
varieties.notes: Small, very sweet 'sugar fig' with a closed eye that resists souring in humid summers; a Southeast favorite, fairly cold-hardy.

varieties.name: Brown Turkey
varieties.notes: Widely adapted, reliable brown fig with a breba plus main crop; resprouts and fruits after winter dieback.

varieties.name: Desert King
varieties.notes: Big early breba crop of green, strawberry-fleshed figs; one of the best where summers are cool or short. Prune lightly.

varieties.name: Black Mission
varieties.notes: The classic purple-black California fig; rich flavor, two crops a year. Large tree that wants long, hot summers.

varieties.name: Kadota
varieties.notes: Green-yellow skin, amber flesh; very sweet but needs real heat to ripen. Excellent for preserves and drying.

varieties.name: Panache
varieties.notes: Striped 'tiger' fig with red, very flavorful flesh. Ripens late and needs a long, hot season.

varieties.name: Violette de Bordeaux
varieties.notes: Small purple-black fig with rich red flesh on a naturally compact plant; an excellent container fig.

varieties.name: Flordaprince
varieties.notes: Very low-chill Florida peach for frost-light winters; ripens in May in warm areas and handles desert heat.

varieties.name: Tropic Snow
varieties.notes: Low-chill white peach with balanced sweet-tart flavor for mild-winter climates; early ripening.

varieties.name: Mid-Pride
varieties.notes: One of the best-flavored yellow peaches for mild winters (Gulf Coast, low desert, coastal California).

varieties.name: Babcock
varieties.notes: Classic sweet, low-acid white peach; low chill yet blooms late enough to dodge many frosts. Widely adapted.

varieties.name: Saturn
varieties.notes: Flat 'donut' white peach, sweet and mild; a low-chill favorite that also grows in moderate climates.

varieties.name: Redhaven
varieties.notes: The benchmark early freestone; reliable, bud-hardy and productive across most of the eastern and central US.

varieties.name: Frost
varieties.notes: Resistant to peach leaf curl, so it skips the winter spray in rainy climates such as the Pacific Northwest.

varieties.name: Contender
varieties.notes: Late-blooming, frost-tolerant buds and bacterial spot resistance; a top peach for cold, frost-prone areas.

varieties.name: Elberta
varieties.notes: The famous old canning and eating peach; large and richly flavored. Widely adapted in moderate winters.

varieties.name: O'Henry
varieties.notes: Large, firm, full-red late peach with superb flavor; good for freezing.

varieties.name: Reliance
varieties.notes: One of the hardiest peaches; flower buds survive about -25 °F, so it crops after severe winters and late cold snaps.

varieties.name: Panamint
varieties.notes: Dependable, intensely flavored red nectarine for warm-winter climates.

varieties.name: Snow Queen
varieties.notes: Sweet, juicy early white nectarine; a long-time low-chill favorite.

varieties.name: Double Delight
varieties.notes: Rich, top-rated yellow nectarine with showy double pink flowers; low chill.

varieties.name: Arctic Star
varieties.notes: Very early, super-sweet low-acid white nectarine with dark red skin.

varieties.name: Fantasia
varieties.notes: Large, popular yellow freestone; tangy when firm-ripe, rich and sweet when left longer. Moderate chill.

varieties.name: Heavenly White
varieties.notes: Very large white nectarine with outstanding sweet-tart, complex flavor.

varieties.name: Independence
varieties.notes: Tangy-sweet red nectarine; winter- and frost-hardy and a very reliable producer.

varieties.name: Harko
varieties.notes: Cold-hardy Canadian nectarine; tolerant of bacterial spot and brown rot. Good for humid, cold-winter areas.

varieties.name: Mericrest
varieties.notes: Very cold- and frost-hardy with late bloom; crops after sub-zero winters. Rich, tangy flavor.

varieties.name: Gold Kist
varieties.notes: The most reliable apricot for mild winters; heavy-bearing, good quality, ripens weeks before Blenheim.

varieties.name: Katy
varieties.notes: Large, sweet, low-acid apricot for warm-winter climates; early.

varieties.name: Blenheim
varieties.notes: Also sold as Royal: the classic sweet, aromatic California apricot for eating, canning and drying. Blooms early.

varieties.name: Tomcot
varieties.notes: Large, reliable apricot from Washington State that keeps producing in frost-prone spring climates.

varieties.name: Moorpark
varieties.notes: Old favorite with exceptionally rich flavor and aroma; for fresh eating and canning.

varieties.name: Puget Gold
varieties.notes: Bred to crop in western Washington; a good choice where spring rain and frost usually ruin apricots.

varieties.name: Harcot
varieties.notes: Canadian apricot with late, frost-hardy bloom and resistance to brown rot; sweet and rich.

varieties.name: Harglow
varieties.notes: Late-blooming Canadian apricot that resists brown rot and cracking; among the best for cold or humid climates.

varieties.name: Methley
varieties.notes: Early, sweet red-fleshed plum; very cold-hardy for a Japanese plum yet low chill. Pollinates other Japanese plums.

varieties.name: Beauty
varieties.notes: Sweet, early plum that crops more reliably than Santa Rosa in cool, rainy springs.

varieties.name: Santa Rosa
varieties.notes: The classic tangy-sweet purple plum; widely adapted, and a common pollinizer for other Japanese plums and pluots.

varieties.name: Satsuma
varieties.notes: Dark red, meaty, mild flesh; superb for jam. Plant with Santa Rosa or Beauty for pollination.

varieties.name: Burgundy
varieties.notes: Sweet, mild maroon plum with a long harvest on a narrow, upright tree.

varieties.name: Stanley
varieties.notes: Hardy, late-blooming, reliable blue prune plum for fresh eating, canning and drying.

varieties.name: Italian
varieties.notes: Rich, sweet freestone prune plum, excellent dried or baked. Vigorous, cold-hardy tree with late bloom.

varieties.name: Toka
varieties.notes: Spicy-sweet American hybrid plum hardy to zone 3; the go-to pollinizer for other cold-climate hybrid plums.

varieties.name: Superior
varieties.notes: Large, firm red plum from Minnesota; bears young and heavily. Plant with Toka for pollination.

varieties.name: Alderman
varieties.notes: Large burgundy plum with sweet, juicy yellow flesh on a vigorous, very hardy tree; needs another hybrid plum nearby.

varieties.name: Flavor King
varieties.notes: Spicy, intensely sweet red-fleshed pluot on a naturally small tree; pollinate with Santa Rosa or another pluot.

varieties.name: Dapple Dandy
varieties.notes: Speckled 'dinosaur egg' pluot with cream-and-red flesh and rich plum-apricot flavor; needs a pollinizer.

varieties.name: Flavor Grenade
varieties.notes: Crisp, green-and-red pluot that hangs on the tree for weeks; pollinate with Santa Rosa or Flavor King.

varieties.name: Minnie Royal
varieties.notes: Low-chill red cherry for mild winters; plant with Royal Lee (they bloom together) or Royal Crimson.

varieties.name: Royal Lee
varieties.notes: Firm, flavorful low-chill cherry; needs Minnie Royal or Royal Crimson as a pollinizer.

varieties.name: Royal Crimson
varieties.notes: Self-fertile low-chill cherry on a compact tree; ripens in May and also pollinates Minnie Royal and Royal Lee.

varieties.name: Stella
varieties.notes: The original self-fertile sweet cherry; large, dark, Lambert-like fruit and a universal pollinizer.

varieties.name: Lapins
varieties.notes: Self-fertile, crack-resistant dark red cherry, sometimes sold as 'self-fertile Bing'.

varieties.name: Bing
varieties.notes: The classic large, dark, sweet cherry; needs a pollinizer such as Van, Rainier or Lapins and is prone to cracking in rain.

varieties.name: Rainier
varieties.notes: Yellow-and-red blush cherry, very sweet; cold-hardy tree. Pollinate with Bing, Van, Lapins or Black Tartarian.

varieties.name: Van
varieties.notes: Very cold-hardy, heavy-bearing Bing-type cherry; pollinizes nearly all sweet cherries.

varieties.name: BlackGold
varieties.notes: Self-fertile, late-blooming black cherry from Cornell that escapes spring frosts; good in the Northeast and Midwest.

varieties.name: Montmorency
varieties.notes: The classic bright-red pie cherry; extremely winter-hardy and very heavy-bearing.

varieties.name: North Star
varieties.notes: Naturally dwarf (8–10 ft) Minnesota pie cherry; hardy to -40 °F, crack-resistant, often bears in year two.

varieties.name: Meteor
varieties.notes: Montmorency-type pie cherry on a small tree; hardy to about -50 °F and blooms a week later.

varieties.name: English Morello
varieties.notes: Late, dark red pie cherry with dark juice; small weeping tree that's easy to pick.

varieties.name: Carmine Jewel
varieties.notes: Saskatchewan dwarf bush cherry (~6 ft), hardy to zone 2; dark, sweet-tart fruit ripening early.

varieties.name: Juliet
varieties.notes: Romance-series bush cherry often rated the best-flavored; sweet enough to eat fresh. Hardy to zone 2.

varieties.name: Romeo
varieties.notes: Romance-series bush cherry, dark red and very flavorful; good for juice. Ripens a bit later. Hardy to zone 2.

varieties.name: Crimson Passion
varieties.notes: Romance-series bush cherry with the highest sugar of the series; large, dark fruit good fresh. Hardy to zone 2.

varieties.name: Dorsett Golden
varieties.notes: Golden Delicious-like apple for very mild winters (Florida, Gulf Coast, low desert); the standard pollinizer for Anna.

varieties.name: Anna
varieties.notes: Crisp low-chill apple that crops even in low desert; plant Dorsett Golden nearby for heavier crops.

varieties.name: Pink Lady
varieties.notes: Very crisp, tart-sweet keeper that needs a long, hot season; ripens a few weeks after Fuji.

varieties.name: Granny Smith
varieties.notes: Tart green keeper for baking and fresh eating; needs a long, warm summer. Long bloom makes it a good pollinizer.

varieties.name: Fuji
varieties.notes: Very sweet, crisp, long-keeping apple; productive in mild-winter climates as well as cold ones.

varieties.name: Gala
varieties.notes: Crisp, sweet, early apple adapted to both cold- and warm-winter areas; an excellent pollinizer.

varieties.name: Golden Delicious
varieties.notes: Reliable all-purpose sweet apple and a widely used pollinizer; adapted to many climates.

varieties.name: Liberty
varieties.notes: Highly resistant to scab, cedar-apple rust, mildew and fire blight; the easiest apple for low-spray humid gardens.

varieties.name: Honeycrisp
varieties.notes: Explosively crisp, juicy University of Minnesota apple; very winter-hardy. Needs another apple for pollination.

varieties.name: Zestar!
varieties.notes: Early, crisp, brown-sugar-tinged Minnesota apple for the far north; ripens in August. Needs a pollinizer.

varieties.name: Haralson
varieties.notes: Extremely hardy Minnesota apple for pies and storage; often bears by year two. A top pick for zones 3–4.

varieties.name: McIntosh
varieties.notes: Aromatic, tender, tangy classic for cold climates; quality suffers where summers are hot.

varieties.name: Bartlett
varieties.notes: The world's favorite pear, also tolerating hot summers; prone to fire blight in humid areas. Ripen picked fruit indoors.

varieties.name: Bosc
varieties.notes: Long-necked russeted pear with superb spicy flavor; great for baking. Very fire-blight prone in warm, wet climates.

varieties.name: Seckel
varieties.notes: Small, very sweet 'sugar pear' with spicy flavor; resists fire blight. Don't rely on Bartlett to pollinate it.

varieties.name: Moonglow
varieties.notes: Soft, juicy dessert pear with good fire-blight resistance; also a good pollinizer for other pears.

varieties.name: Warren
varieties.notes: Buttery, grit-free dessert pear from Mississippi, highly fire-blight resistant; hardy to about -20 °F.

varieties.name: Kieffer
varieties.notes: Tough Asian-European hybrid for canning and cooking; resists fire blight and thrives in hot, humid Southern climates.

varieties.name: Shinseiki
varieties.notes: Bright yellow, crisp, juicy Asian pear that bears young and heavily; ripens on the tree.

varieties.name: 20th Century
varieties.notes: Also sold as Nijisseiki: the classic crisp, juicy, mild yellow Asian pear; keeps well.

varieties.name: Hosui
varieties.notes: Often rated the best-tasting Asian pear: large, sweet, russeted. Plant with another Asian or European pear.

varieties.name: Shinko
varieties.notes: Late, sweet, russeted Asian pear with notable fire-blight resistance; a good pick for humid regions.

varieties.name: Wonderful
varieties.notes: The commercial standard: large, deep red, tangy fruit with fairly hard seeds. Needs long, hot summers to ripen well.

varieties.name: Grenada
varieties.notes: Darker, less tart sport of Wonderful that ripens about a month earlier, before fall rains split fruit.

varieties.name: Eversweet
varieties.notes: Very sweet, soft-seeded, nearly clear non-staining juice; ripens even where summers are cooler.

varieties.name: Parfianka
varieties.notes: Soft edible seeds and complex sweet-tart red arils; often rated the best-flavored pomegranate.

varieties.name: Sweet
varieties.notes: Low-acid, sweet fruit on a small, ornamental tree; better quality than Wonderful in cool-summer areas. Good in containers.

varieties.name: Ambrosia
varieties.notes: Enormous pale-pink fruit with sweet-tart purple juice; a heavy-bearing conversation piece.

varieties.name: A.C. Sweet
varieties.notes: Utah-favored sweet, soft-seeded pomegranate whose ripe fruit hangs without splitting; one of the more cold-hardy picks.

varieties.name: Fuyu
varieties.notes: The standard crisp, non-astringent persimmon, eaten firm like an apple. Self-fertile and nearly pest-free.

varieties.name: Jiro
varieties.notes: Fuyu-type crisp persimmon with squarer, slightly larger fruit; eaten firm.

varieties.name: Izu
varieties.notes: Sweet, non-astringent persimmon on a small tree; ripens about three weeks before Fuyu, good where fall is short.

varieties.name: Hachiya
varieties.notes: Large acorn-shaped persimmon; astringent until jelly-soft, then superb for baking. Needs a hot summer.

varieties.name: Saijo
varieties.notes: Small, elongated, very sweet when soft; considered one of the hardier Asian persimmons, with brilliant fall color.

varieties.name: Prok
varieties.notes: Large, nearly seedless American persimmon with honey-sweet flavor; ripens early enough for northern gardens.

varieties.name: Meader
varieties.notes: Very hardy American persimmon (zone 4) that often sets fruit without a male tree; must be soft-ripe to eat.

varieties.name: Early Golden
varieties.notes: Old early-ripening American persimmon selection with good flavor; a parent of many named varieties.

varieties.name: Shenandoah
varieties.notes: Peterson selection with large fruit, few seeds and mild, creamy flavor. Plant two varieties.

varieties.name: Allegheny
varieties.notes: Peterson selection with rich, well-balanced flavor and good productivity. Needs another variety for pollination.

varieties.name: Susquehanna
varieties.notes: Very large fruit with thick, sweet, buttery flesh and few seeds; late, so best where fall is long.

varieties.name: Sunflower
varieties.notes: Older Kansas selection with large, buttery, yellow fruit. Sometimes sold as self-fertile, but crops far better with a second variety.

varieties.name: Early Red
varieties.notes: Orange-red, pear-shaped fruit that ripens first, extending the short spring season. Fruits only where winter bloom escapes frost.

varieties.name: Big Jim
varieties.notes: Large, round, easy-peel, sweet-tart fruit with excellent flavor; vigorous and productive.

varieties.name: Gold Nugget
varieties.notes: Large orange fruit with firm, apricot-like flesh; self-fertile, so a good single tree or pollinizer.

varieties.name: Champagne
varieties.notes: Yellow-skinned, white-fleshed, juicy subacid fruit; plant with Gold Nugget for best crops.

varieties.name: Vista White
varieties.notes: White-fleshed, very sweet, low-acid loquat, among the best-flavored; bruises easily, so it's a garden-only fruit.

varieties.name: Coolidge
varieties.notes: Reliably self-fertile old California selection; the safest choice when planting a single bush.

varieties.name: Nazemetz
varieties.notes: Large, sweet, pear-shaped fruit with excellent flavor; self-fertile but bears more heavily with a second variety.

varieties.name: Apollo
varieties.notes: New Zealand variety with large, smooth, sweet fruit lacking grittiness; vigorous, self-fertile, a good pollinizer.

varieties.name: Illinois Everbearing
varieties.notes: Hardy, sweet black mulberry fruiting over much of the summer; leafs out late to dodge spring frosts.

varieties.name: Dwarf Everbearing
varieties.notes: Shrubby mulberry that fruits repeatedly in spring and summer; easily kept small or grown in a large pot.

varieties.name: Pakistan
varieties.notes: Very long (3 in+), sweet red-black fruit with little staining juice; for mild-winter, hot-summer climates.

varieties.name: Black Beauty
varieties.notes: Large, glossy, rich black mulberries on a tree or big shrub; self-fertile and low chill.

varieties.name: Li
varieties.notes: The most popular jujube: large round fruit, crisp-sweet when yellow-green or chewy when dried. Self-fertile.

varieties.name: Lang
varieties.notes: Pear-shaped fruit best dried into chewy 'Chinese dates'; plant with Li or another jujube for pollination.

varieties.name: Honey Jar
varieties.notes: Small, extremely sweet, crunchy fruit on a compact tree; superb fresh. Sets more with a second variety.

varieties.name: Shanxi Li
varieties.notes: Largest of the common jujubes; apple-like flavor fresh and sweeter dried. Self-fertile and a good pollinizer.

varieties.name: Sherwood
varieties.notes: Late, crisp, sweet jujube from Louisiana on a narrow, nearly thornless upright tree; good for small yards.

varieties.name: Arbequina
varieties.notes: Compact, precocious, self-fertile Spanish oil olive with small fruit; the usual choice for small yards and large pots.

varieties.name: Mission
varieties.notes: Classic California olive for curing and oil; among the more cold-hardy olives. Large, upright tree.

varieties.name: Manzanillo
varieties.notes: The classic large table olive, cured green or black; spreading tree, moderately cold-hardy.

varieties.name: Koroneiki
varieties.notes: Greek oil olive with tiny fruit and peppery, high-quality oil; frost-tender, so best in mild-winter areas.

varieties.name: Ruby Supreme
varieties.notes: Florida selection with pink-red, sweet, aromatic flesh; good for fresh eating, juice and paste. Frost-tender.

varieties.name: Mexican Cream
varieties.notes: Small, sweet, creamy-white fruit on a compact, upright tree; also sold as Tropical Yellow. Frost-tender.

varieties.name: Strawberry guava
varieties.notes: Small red fruit with tart strawberry notes; hardier (to ~25 °F) than tropical guavas. Invasive in Florida; avoid there.

varieties.name: Lemon guava
varieties.notes: Yellow form of strawberry guava: tangy, lemony fruit on an ornamental shrub; same cold tolerance and invasiveness caution.
